t.1.142.1: Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having awakened, those tigers among men, together with Pṛthā, beheld the superhuman form of Hiḍimbā and were filled with wonder.
t.1.142.2: Then Kuntī, having looked at her and being amazed at the richness of her beauty, spoke gently these sweet words, prefaced with soothing kindness.
t.1.142.5: This great forest that you see, resembling a dark blue cloud, is the dwelling of the rākṣasa Hiḍimba, and mine as well.
t.1.142.4: Whether you are the goddess of this forest or an Apsaras, tell me all of that, and why you are standing here.
t.1.142.6: Know me, O beautiful lady, to be the sister of that lord of the Rākṣasas, sent here, noble lady, by my brother, who wishes to kill you together with your sons.
t.1.142.3: To whom do you belong, you who look like a child of the gods, and who are you, fair-complexioned one? For what purpose, lovely-hipped one, and from where have you come?
t.1.142.7: At the bidding of that cruel-minded one I came here, and I saw your son, mighty in his strength, gleaming with the hue of gold.
t.1.142.8: Then I, impelled by Manmatha, who roams within the fair feelings of all beings, came under the sway of your son.
t.1.142.10: Then, knowing that I was delaying, that man-eater has come himself to kill all these sons of yours.
t.1.142.9: Then I chose your mighty son as my husband, and I tried to carry him away, but I was not able to.
t.1.142.12: Behold these two, the man and the rākṣasa, dragging each other about, of great force, roaring at one another, valiant in battle!
t.1.142.13: As soon as they heard her words, Yudhiṣṭhira sprang up, and so did Arjuna, Nakula, and the valiant Sahadeva.
t.1.142.11: He has been forcibly crushed and dragged away from here by that beloved of mine, your wise and great-souled son.
t.1.142.14: They saw those two locked together, dragging each other back and forth, each longing for victory, like two lions fierce in battle.
t.1.142.15: Clasping each other and dragging one another about, the two of them raised the earth's dust, so that it looked like the smoke of a forest fire.
t.1.142.16: Covered with the dust of the earth and resembling mountains, the two shone like a pair of peaks enveloped in mist.
t.1.142.17: But seeing Bhīma thus being harassed by the Rākṣasa, Pārtha, laughing softly as it were, spoke these words.
t.1.142.20: Watch, sitting by unconcerned; you need not be alarmed. Having come within the grip of my arms, he will never live again.
t.1.142.18: Bhīma, do not be afraid, mighty-armed one! We had no idea that you were locked in combat with that terrible-looking one, for we were fast asleep, worn out by fatigue.
t.1.142.19: I stand ready to help you, Pārtha; I will do battle with the rākṣasa. Nakula and Sahadeva will guard our mother.
t.1.142.21: Bhīma, what is the use of this wicked Rākṣasa living any longer? We must go; it is not possible to stay here long, O tamer of foes.
t.1.142.22: Before the east grows red, before the twilight sets in, for at that dreadful hour the rākṣasas become exceedingly powerful.
t.1.142.23: Hurry, Bhīma, stop playing about! Kill this terrifying demon before he works his magic; put all the strength of your arms into it!
t.1.142.24: Thus addressed by Arjuna, Bhīma lifted up the body of the terrible rākṣasa and swiftly whirled it around more than a hundred times.
t.1.142.26: Or if you consider this rākṣasa a burden in battle, I will give you my help; let him be slain quickly.
t.1.142.25: Fattened in vain on wrongful meats, grown old in vain, vain of mind, you deserve a worthless death; today, for nothing, you shall cease to be.
t.1.142.27: Or else, Vṛkodara, I myself will kill him; you have done your part and are worn out, so rest well for now.
t.1.142.29: As he was being killed by Bhīma, he let out a mighty roar, filling that whole forest, like a drum soaked with water.
t.1.142.28: Hearing those words of his, Bhīmasena, utterly furious, forcibly crushed him against the ground and slew him as one slaughters a sacrificial beast.
t.1.142.30: Binding him tightly with his two arms, the mighty son of Pāṇḍu broke him in the middle, and that mighty one gladdened the Pāṇḍavas.
t.1.142.31: Seeing Hiḍimba slain, those mighty ones, overjoyed, honored Bhīmasena, the tiger among men and tamer of foes.
t.1.142.32: Having honored the great-souled Bhīma of terrible prowess, Arjuna once again spoke these words to Vṛkodara.
t.1.142.33: I think the city is not far from this forest, my lord. Let us go quickly, blessings upon you, so that Suyodhana may not find us out.
t.1.142.34: Then all those scorchers of foes, tigers among men, having said "So be it," set out together with their mother, and so too did the Rākṣasī Hiḍimbā.
